title: Guidelines for Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Courts and Tribunals — Lawyers
pub: Courts of New Zealand / Te Kōti Mana Nui

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: The New Zealand guidance directly supports conditional GenAI assistance under continuing lawyer responsibility. It requires qualified human accuracy checks, applies existing professional and confidentiality duties, and exemplifies the cluster’s ordinary-rule approach by rejecting routine disclosure while preserving courts’ power to require it.
qs: You must check the accuracy of any information you have been provided with by a GenAI chatbot (including legal citations) before using that information in court/tribunal proceedings.
5) Disclosing GenAI use You do not need to disclose use of a GenAI chatbot as a matter of course – unless asked by the court or tribunal.

st.t: Court governance: Assistive use retains human accountability
st.an: The New Zealand guidance directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that GenAI remains assistive and does not displace human professional accountability. It applies existing duties—including the obligation not to mislead the court—and urges caution, although the supplied excerpt does not establish detailed verification, security or disclosure requirements.
qs: The guidelines remind lawyers that their existing professional obligations apply to the use of these new technologies.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition by treating GenAI risks as matters of judicial integrity and continuing professional responsibility. It specifically affirms that lawyers’ existing duties remain in force and calls for caution and practical risk controls, although the supplied excerpt does not substantiate the cluster’s broader lifecycle-governance framework.
qs: The guidelines remind lawyers that their existing professional obligations apply to the use of these new technologies.
They include practical suggestions for minimising the risks and to assist lawyers in complying with their professional obligations when using GenAI chatbots.

st.t: Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
st.an: The guidelines support the cluster’s central distinction between fluent generative capability and legal authority. They recognise useful language-processing functions such as summarisation, while explaining that probabilistic generation lacks an understanding of truth and can produce convincing but fabricated cases, facts and citations. The supplied evidence does not materially address measured performance, agentic systems or allocation of professional responsibility.
qs: These tools have no intrinsic understanding of what any word they output means, nor a conception of truth.
In the legal field, this may lead to GenAI chatbots making up non-existent cases, changing facts, and producing incorrect citations.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The guidance strongly supports the cluster’s core supervised-use proposition: lawyers retain accountability, AI-generated material requires qualified human verification, and confidential information needs safeguards. Its technology-neutral approach and rejection of routine disclosure also align with the synthesis. It does not, however, assess whether verification costs consume AI’s efficiency gains.

st.t: Supervisory accountability: Verification must test substantive support
st.an: The New Zealand guidance accepts the cluster’s core proposition that GenAI does not transfer professional responsibility and that lawyers must verify outputs before relying on them in proceedings. Its required accuracy check covers citations and legal applicability, supporting substantive review rather than reliance on the chatbot’s own assurances, although it does not materially develop the cluster’s emphasis on leadership-level supervision or proportionate sampling.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The guidance supports selective, human-led deployment: it treats generative AI as useful for bounded language-processing tasks but unreliable as an authoritative legal source, requires lawyers to verify outputs before reliance, and preserves professional accountability and confidentiality duties. Its contribution is practical and jurisdiction-specific rather than a material extension of the cluster’s broader proposition.

GenAI chatbots are trained to recognise and reproduce sophisticated patterns in the form of language so they are best suited to natural language processing tasks.

kp.k: Existing professional obligations govern lawyers’ use of generative AI
kp.d: The guidelines respond to increasing GenAI use in Aotearoa New Zealand and advise lawyers representing clients in court and tribunal proceedings. They apply existing duties under the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006 and the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act (Lawyers: Conduct and Client Care) Rules 2008 rather than presenting a separate AI-specific professional regime. Lawyers remain responsible for not misleading courts, information accuracy, suppression compliance and confidentiality.
qs: The guidelines remind lawyers that their existing professional obligations apply to the use of these new technologies.
As officers of the court, lawyers must not mislead the court.
Any use of GenAI chatbots in the context of court and tribunal proceedings must be consistent with the observance of lawyers’ obligations.

kp.k: Lawyers must understand chatbot limitations before using them
kp.d: The guidance recommends basic understanding of GenAI capabilities and limitations before use. It characterises chatbots as probabilistic text generators rather than authoritative search engines, warns that convincing output need not be correct, and states that better prompts cannot eliminate inaccuracies, incompleteness, misleading content or bias. These are guidance statements, not results from a reported empirical study.
qs: Before using GenAI chatbots ensure you have a basic understanding of their capabilities and limitations.
However, even if the output looks convincing, it may not be factually correct.
Even with the best prompts, the output may be inaccurate, incomplete, misleading, or biased.

kp.k: Limited New Zealand training material threatens legal reliability
kp.d: As of 7 December 2023, the guidelines cautiously state that available chatbots appear to have limited training exposure to New Zealand law and procedure, including no significant body of New Zealand cases. They warn that answers may instead rely on inapplicable overseas law or outdated information; the document supplies no quantified assessment of coverage or error rates.
qs: There appears to be limited New Zealand legal information in the training text, and to date the training text does not include a significant body of New Zealand cases.
Information provided by GenAI chatbots is known to be inaccurate, incomplete, or out of date. It may be based on overseas law that does not apply in New Zealand.

kp.k: Qualified human verification remains necessary before court use
kp.d: Lawyers retain responsibility for information supplied to courts and tribunals and must verify chatbot output, including citations, before using it. The guidance warns of fabricated authorities, quotations and facts, misleading legal analysis, and chatbots incorrectly confirming their own accuracy. It therefore requires checking by an appropriately qualified person rather than reliance on the chatbot’s assurances.
qs: You must check the accuracy of any information you have been provided with by a GenAI chatbot (including legal citations) before using that information in court/tribunal proceedings.
Fictitious material produced by GenAI chatbots can seem as though it has been taken from a real source even when it has not.
All information generated by a GenAI chatbot should be checked by an appropriately qualified person for accuracy before it is used or referred to in court or tribunal proceedings

kp.k: Confidentiality and suppression restrict what lawyers may enter
kp.d: The guidelines generally limit chatbot inputs to public-domain information and prohibit entering private, confidential, suppressed or legally privileged information. They warn that some platforms may retain inputs and reuse them in responses to other users. Recommended safeguards include disabling chat history where possible and taking ordinary remedial steps after unintended disclosure, including contacting the registry promptly if a suppression order is breached. Copyright compliance also remains the lawyer’s responsibility.
qs: Generally, you should not enter any information into an AI chatbot that is not already in the public domain.
Do not enter any information that is private, confidential, suppressed or legally privileged information.
You should disable the chat history in AI chatbots if this option is available.
The use of GenAI may raise copyright issues. Compliance with the law of copyright is your responsibility.

kp.k: Protected firm chatbots could change confidentiality precautions
kp.d: The document presents a conditional future possibility: law firms may obtain internal GenAI chatbots that protect confidential, suppressed and private information. Such systems could make this portion of the guidance less relevant, but would not remove lawyers’ obligations or statutory prohibitions concerning privilege, suppression and publication.
qs: In future, law firms may have access to an in-house GenAI chatbot that protects confidential, suppressed, and private information.

If that occurs this portion of the guidelines may be less relevant, however lawyers will continue to be bound by the relevant obligations and statutory prohibitions regarding privilege, suppression, and publication.

kp.k: Bias safeguards must account for New Zealand cultural context
kp.d: Lawyers are advised to consider and address ethical issues, especially biases inherited from training data. The guidelines specifically warn that chatbots generally fail to account for New Zealand’s cultural context and Māori and Pasifika values and practices. They acknowledge algorithmic countermeasures against bias and harmful content but state that these do not eliminate the risks.
qs: Have regard to ethical issues – particularly biases and the need to address them.
GenAI chatbots generally do not account for New Zealand’s cultural context, nor specific cultural values and practices of Māori and Pasifika.
However, these countermeasures do not eliminate the risk of biases or harmful or dangerous information being included in responses.

kp.k: Routine disclosure is unnecessary unless courts require it
kp.d: The guidance does not require lawyers to disclose chatbot use as a matter of course. It states that following the guidelines, particularly accuracy checking, should adequately address the key risks, while preserving courts’ and tribunals’ ability to ask for or require disclosure.
qs: You do not need to disclose use of a GenAI chatbot as a matter of course – unless asked by the court or tribunal.
Provided these guidelines have been followed (in particular, checking for accuracy), the key risks associated with GenAI should have been adequately addressed.
However, a court or tribunal may ask or require lawyers to disclose GenAI use.

kp.k: Text transformation is suitable, factual answers require caution
kp.d: The guidelines identify natural-language processing as chatbots’ best-suited task category, including summarisation, changes of tone or format, and generating text in requested formats. They also acknowledge that chatbots can provide useful topic information and answers, but qualify this usefulness with warnings about hallucination and inaccuracy.
qs: These tasks include summarising text by making it shorter or changing its tone or format; and generating new text in a requested format.
This means they can often provide useful information about a certain topic and answers to specific questions.
However, when used for these purposes it is important to remember that GenAI chatbots can ‘hallucinate’ and provide incorrect or inaccurate information.

kp.k: Synthetic multimedia raises evidential authenticity concerns
kp.d: Beyond chatbot text, the guidelines warn that multimedia-generating AI can produce apparently authentic but fake images, audio or video. They identify potential defamation, misinformation and disinformation, and flag authenticity concerns when such multimedia is used as evidence, without reporting particular incidents or measured prevalence.
qs: This technology allows for the creation of multimedia that appear authentic but are fake.
These multimedia are known as ‘deepfakes’ and can be defamatory or spread dangerous misinformation or disinformation.
Concerns may arise over the authenticity of multimedia when used in evidence.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Courts of New Zealand describe growing chatbot use and identify text processing as a suitable application, while retaining lawyers’ existing professional responsibilities.
pts.d: The institutional guidance states that GenAI use in the New Zealand legal context is increasing. It identifies summarisation, changes of tone or format, and generation of text in requested formats as suitable tasks. It does not quantify uptake, productivity gains, costs or employment effects. Its approach is supervised assistance rather than direct reliance on unchecked output: existing duties to courts, clients and others continue to apply.

pts.k: Chatbots introduce risks of fabricated legal material, incorrect advice and jurisdictional mismatch, requiring qualified human verification.
pts.d: The guidance attributes these risks to probabilistic text generation, training-data limitations and limited coverage of New Zealand law. It says convincing output may contain fictitious cases, citations or quotations, factual errors, inapplicable overseas law or outdated information. Asking the chatbot to confirm accuracy is not a substitute for checking. Lawyers remain responsible for information submitted to courts and tribunals.

pts.k: Entering information into chatbots can expose protected material; future protected in-house systems may reduce this particular risk.
pts.d: The guidance warns that some systems may retain inputs and use them in responses to other users, potentially making confidential, privileged, private or suppressed information public. It also flags possible copyright issues. Its future-facing claim is conditional: law firms may obtain in-house chatbots that protect information, making this portion of the guidance less relevant without removing legal obligations.

pts.k: Training-data bias and limited cultural coverage can affect chatbot output; synthetic multimedia can create evidentiary authenticity concerns.
pts.d: The guidance states that chatbot responses reflect training-data bias and misinformation and generally do not account for New Zealand’s cultural context or Māori and Pasifika values and practices. It says technical countermeasures do not eliminate biased or harmful responses. Separately, it identifies the ability to generate apparently authentic but fake multimedia as a potential source of defamation, misinformation and doubts about evidence.

pts.k: The guidance considers compliance, particularly accuracy checking, sufficient to address key risks without routine disclosure of chatbot use.
pts.d: This is a qualified institutional judgment and procedural position, not a measured finding that verification eliminates every risk. Courts and tribunals retain the ability to ask for or require disclosure.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on judicial authority, existing New Zealand professional rules and qualitative explanations of technology, not empirical performance evidence.
pts.d: The document is institutional guidance owned by the Artificial Intelligence Advisory Group and approved by the listed judicial and tribunal leadership bodies. It cites the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006 and the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act (Lawyers: Conduct and Client Care) Rules 2008 for lawyers’ obligations, including duties to uphold the rule of law and not mislead courts. Its technical claims are supported by explanations of probabilistic generation, training data and platform-dependent retention. It supplies no adoption statistics, benchmarks, measured hallucination rates, named sanctions cases or studies demonstrating the effectiveness of its safeguards. Statements about limited New Zealand training coverage are expressly qualified by language such as “appear” and “appears”.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern tools available on 7 December 2023; future protected systems are an undated possibility.
pts.d: The guidance was first issued and last updated on 7 December 2023. Present-tense assessments concern then-available chatbots, including ChatGPT, Google Bard and Bing Chat, rather than all future legal AI. Output quality is conditioned on training, data reliability and prompting, but good prompts do not guarantee correctness. Information retention depends on platform and privacy settings. Verification must occur before courtroom use; routine nondisclosure is conditional on following the guidance and the absence of a court or tribunal request. No timetable is supplied for protected in-house systems.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are courtroom lawyers, courts and tribunals, clients and other parties, and people whose information or cultural context may be mishandled.
pts.d: The guidance addresses lawyers representing clients before the New Zealand courts and tribunals listed in the document, across senior, district and specialist courts and civil, administrative and disciplinary tribunals. Lawyers must understand limitations, protect information and verify output while retaining accountability. Courts and tribunals face risks to accurate submissions, authentic evidence and the administration of justice. Clients, opposing parties and opposing counsel are affected by confidentiality and accuracy duties; people protected by suppression, privacy or privilege may suffer disclosure harms. Māori and Pasifika are specifically identified in relation to cultural limitations. Law firms are mentioned as possible future users of protected in-house systems. The source makes no differentiated prediction about firm size, staffing, fees, competitive market shares or access to justice.
